items.evidence: The overview's first section after the title is "## The bottom line", which runs "**1. What FRUS answers directly** —", then "**2. Where FRUS points for the rest** —", then "**3. What this request cannot get from FRUS** —", in that order; "Scope" and "Decisions this needs from you" follow, and "## Findings" comes only after them. The collection's introductionText restates the same three parts in the same order ("What FRUS answers directly: ... Where FRUS points for the rest: ... What this request cannot get from FRUS: ...").

Every figure names its set and base in words: "22 documents chosen from about 4,100 in which Cuba is named five or more times, among about 12,300 documents that name it at all in the 553 volumes indexed"; "621 of the same 4,100 documents carry at least one such citation"; "the index records a source for 1 of 309 documents"; "the 177 indexed documents dated in the 1990s include none that names Cuba"; "before 1947 only 10 documents pair it with Cuba" and "10 of 40 sampled documents use it in any other sense"; "literal in 39 of 40 evenly spaced sample documents"; "documents per thousand in each decade named Cuba, from about 62 per thousand in the 1870s, to 17 in the 1940s, to 114 in the 1960s"; "2,982 of 6,124 documents naming Cuba from 1958 on sit in a single Cuba cluster, and none of the 1,240 from 1870 to 1899 do". Finding 6's shares are in words with their base ("the share of documents that use defence or Soviet vocabulary close to a mention of Cuba rises from between one in five and one in three before 1958 to about four in five from 1958", the scanned set of 4,100 named in How this was done). No "%" appears; the one "per cent" is inside a quoted document, "a reduction from 20 to 25 per cent of Cuba's quota", the document's own words. NARA entries and identifiers and the decimal file class 837 are labels, not counts.

Every document is cited in the printed-edition form with a link, e.g. "Foreign Relations of the United States, 1958–1960, Cuba, Volume VI, Document 535, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1958-60v06/d535", "Foreign Relations of the United States, Diplomatic Papers, 1934, The American Republics, Volume V, Document 170, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1934v05/d170", "Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1874, Document 552, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1874/d552"; the 1898 war message, which the printed edition carries as an unnumbered chapter item, is cited as "Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1898, the President's message to Congress, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1898/ch83", edition, year and link. The two documents the bottom line quotes without an inline cite (the 16 October 1962 transcript, the 1959–60 sugar documents) are cited in full in Findings 4 and 5. Stripping the links from the file and searching for "frus" finds nothing, so no bare id pair and nothing cited by title alone.

The zeros are stated as searches with terms, volumes and controls: "(c) The years after 1988: the 177 indexed documents dated in the 1990s include none that names Cuba ... a test search for a nonsense word returned nothing and a search for “Department of State” returned documents in every one of the 553 volumes, so the absence is not a failure of the search"; "(d) ... the phrase “national security” itself: before 1947 only 10 documents pair it with Cuba, and in the short stretches of text around the phrase that I examined it appears in the name of a statute, a Cuban declaration or unrelated business; after 1946 the phrase is mostly the name of the National Security Council (10 of 40 sampled documents use it in any other sense)"; and (b) rests on part 2's count, "the index records a source for 1 of 309 documents, and the footnote channel has no entry before December 1910". How this was done adds the literal-match check ("39 of 40 evenly spaced sample documents"). The one part stated as an assertion is (a), trade statistics: "the data I used do not index the Commerce or Treasury trade statistics that would show it, so I name no shelf for them", a statement of what the data are rather than a search run.

The overview holds no SQL, no table or column name and no file path (a search for SELECT/WHERE/JOIN, underscore-joined names, .csv/.py/.json/.tsv and /Users or /tmp finds nothing). The only FRUS volume/document ids are inside the history.state.gov links the citations require; with the links stripped, no "frus…" string remains. The other numbers are NARA entries and identifiers ("entry A1 3053, NARA identifier 27022950", "file-unit identifier 177380726, series 603720") and the decimal file class "837", none a volume_id/document_id pair.

judge:v1.rankingReason: v1: clean on all five items, spans 1874–1981 in six findings on 22 documents and 31 passages with every cite complete and linked, a bottom line a historian can use on its own, and the sharpest decisions list (each with its consequence stated). v3: the richest evidence (23 documents, 35 passages, the 1944–45 base talks, Dulles's "strategic concept", the 1963 minimum aim) and the fullest shelves and limits section, but six cites give correspondents and a date in place of the document number ("Mr. Fish to Mr. Cushing, 6 February 1874"), the bottom line defers all its cites to the findings, and it is the densest read. v4: every cite complete and linked, controls carried inside the limits section, and the 1974 "no vital interests" memo is a telling find, but it prints no document between 1945 and 1959, so the fusion of defence and sugar that the other three show is missing and the span is five findings on 16 documents. v2: a sound corpus-controlled method (a random sample of 300 per decade) and the 1933–1954 sugar hinge, but about a dozen bottom-line cites carry no link ("1902, Document 313; 1903, Document 331"), only 16 documents, the 1874 Fish instruction was missed, and the account stops at 1980 while the controls sit in the method section rather than beside the zero.

AND document_id=?`. The one exploratory `document_id IN (...)` query in queries.log pins both sides to `frus1934v05` and was re-issued on rowid in the next line.

score:v1.notes: All four named files are present (memo.md 269 lines, overview.md, collection.fruscollection, queries.log), plus 65 retrieved documents under docs/ and the scripts and outputs the memo names. The session did open the vector artifacts (semantic-vectors-index.json, the binary, the map and its index, one Tier-2 shard and .generation), so V1–V6 were scored. Compliance 39/40 = 97.5%. Independent verification: the coverage row, both controls, all twelve N01 decade rows, the pre-1947 'national security' count (10), the 1870–1899 Havana-only count (240), the 1990s absence (177 dated, 0 hits), the earliest external citation (1910-12-06), the Ed2 fold, the provenance digest across six artifacts, the segment decode (314,616 rows, ch83 absent), four Hamming distances, seven NAID resolutions and the five pre-1906 series identifiers all reproduce; 32 of 32 quotations, 31 of 31 excerpts and 37 of 37 overview quotation strings are verbatim in body_text. The one violation is V6: the volume-centroid cosines in memo V3 are neither passed through the index's scoreCalibration offsets nor labelled raw. Borderline calls recorded in the evidence rather than scored against the run: V1 names digests as equal and the named digest is correct for every artifact, but the shards manifest was not opened and the comparison code is not in the kept vec.py; P6's log is honest about its elisions but vec.py's checks, vec_dup.py and arch1–3.py keep no output file and the A07/A08/A12 JSON heredocs were not kept; the overview renders the N01/N05 shares as word ratios ('four in five', '62 per thousand') with denominators only in the memo, which I treated as O2's domain rather than a P5/R2 failure; 'four grounds' (finding 1) is the one overview figure without a memo line and is a reading of the cited 1898 message; O1's only id-pair strings are inside the public history.state.gov citation URLs. E3 is not_applicable because cross_references was never queried (only its schema was listed).

The other 33 (8 inline in the bottom line, 7 inline in the findings, 18 block quotes) were each checked by the guide's rule (lower-case, strip to [a-z0-9], split at ellipses, segments in order) against header||dateline||source_note||body_text of the exact pair the overview's URL names, or, for the seven inline quotations with no citation beside them, the pair the memo's trace table gives (Q03, Q10, Q13, Q14, Q16, Q18, Q20, Q26): 33 of 33 found, each as one segment. All 31 collection excerpts were checked the same way against their own volumeId/documentId: 31 of 31 found. The four single-quoted phrases in the collection's notes and prose ('economic and defense reasons', 'retaliatory instruments', 'subsidiary and lesser', 'intolerable and not acceptable') are also in their documents. refute:v1.miscitationDetails: None. Every quotation is credited to the pair that holds it, and every printed edition citation resolves to the URL's pair: the document number in each citation equals the index's document_number for that document_id (552, 498, 273, 333, 241, 170, 154, 134, 420, 440, 331, 362, 532, 535, 567, 18, 21, 205, 18, 129, 10); ch83 is cited as 'the President's message to Congress' and its header is 'Message' with body 'To the Congress of the United States: ... the neighboring island of Cuba', dated by the index 1898-04-12. The 12 volume titles from 1933 onward equal the manifest titles exactly (whitespace-collapsed). The four 19th/early-20th-century citations use the short form 'Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1874/1898/1902/1918' where the manifest title is the long 'Transmitted to Congress, With the Annual Message of the President, December 7, 1874' form; each resolves uniquely (one frus1874, one frus1898; the 1902 appendices and 1918 supplements carry 'Appendix'/'Supplement' in their titles, which the citations do not), so not a mis-citation. The memo's own attribution of speakers (Fish, Woodford, Rusk, JFK, McNamara, Rubottom, Gates, Anderson/Dillon) was not re-read at the sentence; the overview's inline paraphrases match the memo's section 4 table.

(3) Records Relating to the Cuban Missile Crisis: lot 65D438, entry A1 3053, NAID 27022950, RG 59, 1962-1963, 'Restricted - Partly' - confirmed (28 came-from documents 1958-89; 13 pointed-at rows). (4) The Secretary's and the Under Secretary's Memorandums of Conversation: entry A1 1566, NAID 602231, 1953-1964, 'Unrestricted' - confirmed; lots 64D199 and 65D330 both resolve to it (11 + 11 came-from documents). (5) Subject Files of the Office of the Special Assistant on Communism, Bureau of Inter-American Affairs: lot 62D24, entry A1 3148, NAID 2363836, 1958-1961 (coverage 1956-1961), 'Restricted - Partly' - confirmed (14 came-from). (6) Files Pertaining to Operation Mongoose, Office of the Coordinator of Cuban Affairs: lot 66D501, entry UD-UP 293-B, NAID 648748, 1963-1965 (coverage 1960-1999), 'Unrestricted' - confirmed (12 came-from). (7) Records Relating to National Security Council Policy Papers: lot 66D95, entry A1 1586E, NAID 2839192, 1947-1979, 'Restricted - Partly' - confirmed (28 pointed-at rows in 24 documents, the most-cited lot). (8) Second claimant Subject Files, entry A1 1586F (NAID 2839193, 1947-1965) - confirmed in lot-claimants-index.json. (9) Records Relating to Sugar: lot 65D212, entry UD-UP 215, NAID 27022874, inclusive 1955-1962, coverage 1932-1962, 'Restricted - Fully' - confirmed (2 pointed-at rows). (10-14) Presidential-library collections, confirmed as document_sources series_name values in the scope: Kennedy Library National Security Files (225, plus 81 spelled 'NSF'), Johnson Library National Security File (69), Carter Library National Security Affairs (215), Nixon Presidential Materials NSC Files (118), Eisenhower Library Whitman File (66); and in channel two Carter NSA 134, Kennedy NSF 65, Johnson NSF 26, Nixon NSC Files 20 rows.
